documentNotes.title: 2005 Semi-Final Exam — Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
AAPT / AIP — United States Physics Team 2005.

DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN

- Work Part A first. You have 90 minutes to complete all four problems.
- After you have completed Part A, you may take a break.
- Then work Part B. You have 90 minutes to complete both problems.
- Show all your work. Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper. Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem. For example: Doe, Jamie; A1 – 1/3.
- A hand-held calculator may be used. Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. You may use only the basic functions found on a simple scientific calculator. Calculators may not be shared. Cell phones, PDA’s, or cameras may not be used during the exam or while the exam papers are present. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas.
- Questions with the same point value are not necessarily of the same difficulty.
- Do not discuss the contents of this exam with anyone until after the submission deadline.
- Good luck!

problems.statement:
[[figure:p1-fig1]]

Each of the seven resistors in the network above has the same resistance $R$.

figures.alt: Seven-resistor network between terminalsA andB, with labelsR1 throughR7.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: If an ideal battery of emf $\mathcal E$ and no internal resistance is connected across the points labeled A and B, what is the current $I_j$ that flows in the $j^{th}$ resistor $R_j$ (for each of the seven resistors)?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What equivalent resistor could be used to replace the network so that the same current flowed from the battery?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: If the resistor labeled $R_4$ was removed and replaced by a capacitor with capacitance $C$, what would the charge be on the capacitor after the circuit had been connected to the battery for a very long time?

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
Since $R_3$ and $R_6$ are in series, $I_3=I_6$. Since $R_2$ and $R_5$ are in series, $I_2=I_5$. By symmetry, the current through $R_3$ and $R_6$ must be the same as the current through $R_2$ and $R_5$ since the current through A = the current through B and this current splits into two branches — one with a resistance of $2R$ and the other with a resistance of $R$. Therefore,

$$I_2=I_3=I_5=I_6\tag{A1-1}$$

and $I_1=I_7$. (A1-2)

By the junction rule,

$$I_1=I_2+I_4.\tag{A1-3}$$

Applying the loop rule from A to B across the top of the circuit,

$$\epsilon=I_1R+2I_2R.\tag{A1-4}$$

Applying the loop rule from A to B going through $R_1$, $R_4$, and $R_7$ yields

$$\epsilon=I_1R+I_4R+I_1R.\tag{A1-5}$$

Substitute (A1-3) into (A1-4) and (A1-5).

$$\epsilon=3I_2R+I_4R\tag{A1-6}$$

and $\epsilon=2I_2R+3I_4R$. (A1-7)

Subtract (A1-7) from (A1-6) to obtain

$$I_2=2I_4.\tag{A1-8}$$

Substitute into (A1-6) or (A1-7) to find that

$$I_4=\frac\epsilon{7R}.\tag{A1-9}$$

Then, from (A1-8) and (A1-1),

$$I_2=I_3=I_5=I_6=\frac{2\epsilon}{7R}.\tag{A1-10}$$

Using (A1-3) and (A1-2),

$$I_1=I_7=\frac{3\epsilon}{7R}.\tag{A1-11}$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
$$I_{\rm battery}=\frac\epsilon{R_{\rm equiv}}\tag{A1-12}$$

and $I_{\rm battery}=I_1+I_2$. (A1-13)

Therefore, by substituting (A1-10) and (A1-11) into (A1-12) and (A1-13),

$$\frac\epsilon{R_{\rm equiv}}=\frac{5\epsilon}{7R}.\tag{A1-14}$$

Thus, $R_{\rm equiv}=7R/5$. (A1-15)

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
After a very long time, no current will flow through the branch of the circuit with the capacitor. Therefore, $R_1$, $R_2$, and $R_5$ are in series and $R_3$, $R_6$, and $R_7$ are in series. The current through the top branch and the current through the bottom branch will then be

$$I=\frac\epsilon{3R}.\tag{A1-16}$$

The voltage drop across $R_1$ is $IR$ and the voltage drop across $R_3$ and $R_6$ is $2IR$. Thus, the voltage drop across the capacitor is $2IR-IR=IR$.

Using (A1-16),

$$V_{\rm cap}=\frac\epsilon3.\tag{A1-17}$$

The charge on the capacitor is $Q=CV_{\rm cap}=C\epsilon/3$. (A1-18)

problems.statement:
A sample of water of mass 0.0360 kg and temperature $100^\circ$C is added to an enclosed container of volume 2.00 m$^3$ that contains air at a pressure of $1.00\times10^5$ Pa and a temperature of 500 K. Assume both air and steam can be treated as ideal gases and that all of the water vaporizes. What is the final temperature and pressure inside the container?

Possibly useful information:

| Molar Heat Capacities | Air | Steam |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $C_V$ (at constant volume) | 20.8 J/(mol·K) | 27.9 J/(mol·K) |
| $C_P$ (at constant pressure) | 29.1 J/(mol·K) | 36.2 J/(mol·K) |

$L_V$ (Latent heat of vaporization) $=2.26\times10^6$ J/kg.

Molar mass of water $=18.0$ g/mol.

solution.statement:
Source note: the numerical substitution below interchanges the initial air and steam temperatures. The printed equation and the printed final answer are both retained.

Vaporizing the water will require energy:

$$\Delta U_{\rm vap}=mL_v=(0.0360\text{ kg})(2.26\times10^6\text{ J/kg})=81.4\text{ kJ}.\tag{A2-1}$$

We find that we have $\frac{0.0360\text{ kg}}{0.018\text{ kg/mol}}=2.0\text{ mol}$ of water.

Using $pV=nRT$, we find that we have 48.1 mol of air.

Since the volume is constant, the change in internal energy of the air and of the steam are given by

$$\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T.\tag{A2-2}$$

The total change in internal energy of the system must be zero:

$$\Delta U_{\rm vap}+\Delta U_{\rm steam}+\Delta U_{\rm air}=0.\tag{A2-3}$$

Substituting (A2-1) and (A2-2) into (A2-3):

$$81.4\text{ kJ}+(nC_V\Delta T)_{\rm steam}+(nC_V\Delta T)_{\rm air}=0.\tag{A2-4}$$

$$81.4\text{ kJ}+(2.0\text{ mol})(27.9\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)})(T_f-500\text{ K})+(48.1\text{ mol})(20.8\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)})(T_f-373\text{ K})=0.$$

$$T_{\rm final}=416\text{ K}.\tag{A2-5}$$

There are a total of 2.0 mol + 48.1 mol = 50.1 mol of gas in the container, so from the ideal gas law,

$$p=\frac{nRT}{V}=\frac{(50.1\text{ mol})(8.31\text{ J/mol}\cdot\text{K})(416\text{ K})}{2.00\text{ m}^3}=86.7\text{ kPa}.\tag{A2-6}$$

problems.statement:
A plane wave traveling in the positive $z$-direction can be described by the following wavefunction: $\psi(z,t)=A\sin(kz-\omega t+\phi)$, where $A$ (the amplitude) and $\phi$ are constants, $k=2\pi/\lambda$, $\omega=2\pi f$, $f$ is the frequency, and $\lambda$ is the wavelength. The factor $(kz-\omega t+\phi)$ is called the phase of the wave. The following relation may be useful:

$$\sin\alpha+\sin\beta=2\cos\left[\tfrac12(\alpha-\beta)\right]\sin\left[\tfrac12(\alpha+\beta)\right].$$

figures.alt: SourceS at heightd/2 above reflecting surface and screen at distanceL with pointX and yaxis.
Two coherent sourcesS above and below air-material interface, separationd, refractive indexn and screen at distanceL.

solution.statement: Source note: (A3-2) repeats the label r1. Equation (A3-5) prints minus pi, followed by the statement n=1 and the final first-maximum expression; these printed forms are mutually inconsistent and are retained. The phase sign also changes between (A3-9) and (A3-11).

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
We can assume that there is an image of the source S in the perfectly reflecting surface located a distance $d/2$ beneath the surface. The problem then reduces to one of two point sources a distance $d$ apart creating an interference pattern on a screen a located a distance $L\gg d$ away from the sources. We are informed that the midpoint on the screen, $y=0$, is an interference minimum. Since this would be an interference maximum for two point sources which are in phase, then we can conclude that the phase of the reflected wave is shifted by an amount $\pi$, so that the location of interference maxima and interference minima are switched relative to the “normal” presentation. Consequently, the location of the first maximum is $y=\lambda L/2d$.

In the event that you forgot the formula, you will need to derive it.

The distance from the object point source to a point on the screen is

$$r_1=\sqrt{(y-d/2)^2+L^2}\approx L\left(1+\frac{(y-d/2)^2}{2L^2}\right).\tag{A3-1}$$

The distance from the image point source to a point on the screen is

$$r_1=\sqrt{(y+d/2)^2+L^2}\approx L\left(1+\frac{(y+d/2)^2}{2L^2}\right).\tag{A3-2}$$

The path length difference is then

$$r_2-r_1\approx\frac{yd}{L},\tag{A3-3}$$

where the approximation is true for $L\gg y+d/2$.

The relative phase shift due to the path length difference is found by dividing through by the wavelength and multiplying by $2\pi$, so

$$\Delta\phi_{\rm pld}=2\pi\frac{yd}{\lambda L}.\tag{A3-4}$$

There is an additional phase shift of $\pi$ from the reflection, so that the overall phase difference between the waves is

$$\Delta\phi=2\pi\frac{yd}{\lambda L}-\pi.\tag{A3-5}$$

Constructive interference occurs when $\Delta\phi=2n\pi$, where $n$ is an integer; the smallest value for $y$ with constructive interference happens when $n=1$, or

$$y=\frac{\lambda L}{2d}.\tag{A3-6}$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
For the wave from the source above the boundary:

$$\psi_1=A\sin(kz-\omega t+\phi).\tag{A3-7}$$

The wave below the boundary travels in a medium that (1) doesn’t affect $\omega$ or $\phi$, but (2) scales $k$ according to $k\to nk$, since the wave velocity is changed but the frequency is unaffected. Consequently the wave equation from the second source is

$$\psi_2=A\sin(nkz-\omega t+\phi).\tag{A3-8}$$

The distance $z$ is the same for both, and is approximately equal to $L$ for $L\gg d$.

Adding the two waves in (A3-7) and in (A3-8) and making use of the given trigonometric identity yields

$$\psi_1+\psi_2=2A\cos\left[\frac{(n-1)kL}{2}\right]\sin\left[\frac{(n+1)kL}{2}-\omega t+\phi\right].\tag{A3-9}$$

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
The intensity is proportional to the wave-function squared, or

$$I\propto\psi^2.\tag{A3-10}$$

The time average is found by integrating the above expression over one period and then dividing by the period, or

$$\langle I\rangle\propto4A^2\cos^2\left[\frac{(n-1)kL}{2}\right]\frac\omega{2\pi}\int_{\rm period}\sin^2\left[\frac{(n+1)kL}{2}-\omega t-\phi\right]dt.\tag{A3-11}$$

Everything inside the sin function can be written compactly as

$$\sin^2\left[\frac{(n+1)kL}{2}-\omega t-\phi\right]=\sin^2[\alpha-\omega t].\tag{A3-12}$$

A change of variables to try would be

$$u=\alpha-\omega t.\tag{A3-13}$$

Then the expression for the time-averaged intensity becomes

$$\langle I\rangle\propto\cos^2\left[\frac{(n-1)kL}{2}\right]\int_{\rm period}\sin^2u\,du,\tag{A3-14}$$

where we have conveniently swallowed all constants into the proportionality. The integral is fairly easy, but it doesn’t matter, since it is also a constant independent of $k$ or $L$. So it can be swallowed as well, leaving

$$\langle I\rangle\propto\cos^2\left[\frac{(n-1)kL}{2}\right].\tag{A3-15}$$

This is true for all values of the argument of the cosine function, including the value that maximizes the cosine function, so

$$\langle I\rangle=I_0\cos^2\left[\frac{(n-1)kL}{2}\right]\tag{A3-16}$$

gives us the required relation for $\langle I\rangle_{\max}$.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
[[figure:p3-fig1]]

A point source $S$ of monochromatic electromagnetic radiation of wavelength $\lambda$ is located a distance $d/2$ above a perfectly reflecting surface represented by the solid horizontal line in the diagram above. An interference pattern is formed on the screen a distance $L$ from the source, $L\gg d$. The point $y=0$, at the intersection of the screen and the reflecting surface, represented by an X in the diagram, is an interference minimum. Point X is on the surface of the material.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: The first bright band is located a distance $y_b$ above point X. Find $y_b$.

sections.title: b.–c.
sections.statement:
[[figure:p3-fig2]]

The reflecting surface is replaced by a material that does not reflect but transmits without loss of amplitude. The material has index of refraction $n$. One source is placed a distance $d/2$ above the air-material interface. The other source is embedded in the material a distance $d/2$ below the interface. The two sources are in phase, coherent, emit electromagnetic radiation of the same monochromatic wavelength $\lambda$ in vacuum, and are both located a distance $L$ from a screen, $L\gg d$. Assume that the wave amplitude $A$ due to each source individually is the same at point X and that the wave from the lower source travels entirely in the material.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the resultant wavefunction at point X as a function of time?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Let $I_0$ denote the maximum intensity reaching point X, which occurs when $n=1$. Derive an expression for the time averaged intensity of the electromagnetic radiation at point X as a function of $n$, $I_0$, $L$, and $\lambda$.

problems.statement: Just like electrostatic fields, gravitational fields obey Gauss’s Law. One of the arguments for dark matter in the universe is the observation that the velocity of stars orbiting far from the center of the galaxy is approximately constant. This requires a spherically symmetric mass distribution which the visible stars do not have. Let the mass density of the galaxy be $\rho(r)=Ar^n$ where $A$ is a constant, $r$ is the distance from the center of galaxy, and the power $n$ is as yet undetermined.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Show that the total mass $M$ enclosed by a sphere of radius $R$ is $M(R)=CR^{n+3}$ and find the constant $C$ in terms of given variables and known constants.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement:
You may use $M(R)=CR^{n+3}$, with $C$ unspecified, for the remaining parts of this problem.

Find the magnitude of the gravitational force on a star of mass $m$ which has a circular orbit of radius $R$ about the center of this galaxy.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Find the orbital velocity $v$ of this star.

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: What power $n$ is required by the observation that $v$ is constant?

parts.label: e.
parts.statement: If the mass density were $\rho(r)\approx0$ for $r>R$, a reasonable assumption based on the observed visible star distribution, what would be the orbital velocity of a star with $r>R$? Let $M_0=$ the total mass of the galaxy.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
The mass of a spherical shell of radius $r$ and thickness $dr$ is

$$\rho(r)4\pi r^2dr=Ar^n4\pi r^2dr=Ar^{n+2}4\pi dr.\tag{A4-1}$$

To find the total mass enclosed by a sphere of radius $R$, we add up the mass of all of the spherical shells:

$$M(R)=\int_0^RAr^{n+2}4\pi dr=\frac{4\pi AR^{n+3}}{n+3}=CR^{n+3}\tag{A4-2}$$

where $C=\frac{4\pi A}{n+3}$. (A4-3)

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
Gauss’s Law applied to a spherical shell of radius $R$ gives us

$$\oint\vec g\cdot d\vec A=-4\pi GM_{\rm enclosed}.\tag{A4-4}$$

By symmetry, $g$ is constant over the surface of the spherical shell. $g$ is radially inward, so

$$\oint\vec g\cdot d\vec A=-g4\pi R^2.\tag{A4-5}$$

When we substitute (A4-5) into (A4-4) and substitute (A4-2) for $M_{\rm enclosed}$, we obtain

$$-g4\pi R^2=-4\pi GCR^{n+3}.\tag{A4-6}$$

Solving for $g$,

$$g=GCR^{n+1}.\tag{A4-7}$$

The gravitational force on a star of mass $m$ is then

$$F_{\rm grav}=mg=mGCR^{n+1}.\tag{A4-8}$$

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
Applying Newton’s second law to the circular motion of the star, we find that

$$F_{\rm grav}=\frac{mv^2}{R}.\tag{A4-9}$$

Substituting (A4-8) into (A4-9) yields

$$mGCR^{n+1}=\frac{mv^2}{R}.\tag{A4-10}$$

$$v=\sqrt{GCR^{n+2}}.\tag{A4-11}$$

sections.title: d.
sections.statement: If $v$ is constant, then $R^{n+2}=R^0$, so $n=-2$. (A4-12)

sections.title: e.
sections.statement:
Apply Gauss’s Law to a spherical shell of radius $r$, where $r>R$. Here, the mass enclosed is $M_0$.

$$-g4\pi r^2=-4\pi GM_0.\tag{A4-13}$$

$$g=\frac{GM_0}{r^2}.\tag{A4-14}$$

Substituting into (A4-9)

$$\frac{mGM_0}{r^2}=\frac{mv^2}{r}.\tag{A4-15}$$

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{GM_0}{r}}.\tag{A4-16}$$

problems.statement:
A length of wire is formed into a ring of radius $b$ and total charge $Q$ that is distributed uniformly around the ring. The ring is in the $x$-$y$ plane and centered on the origin as shown in the accompanying diagram. $\hat i$, $\hat j$, and $\hat k$ are unit vectors in the $x$, $y$, and $z$ directions respectively. Assume the potential vanishes at infinity.

[[figure:p5-fig1]]

figures.alt: Uniformly charged ringQ radiusb in xyplane with zaxis and unit vectorsi,j,k.
Official-key charged-ring geometry with unit vectors.
Ring elementdQ with radiusb, positionr andz, electric and magnetic contributionsdE,dB and anglephi/theta.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
By symmetry, the $x$ and $y$ components of the electric field from different parts of the ring will cancel:

$$E_x=E_y=0.$$

Therefore, we need to add up the $z$-components of the electric field from the various parts of the ring:

[[figure:p5-fig2]]

The electric field due to an infinitesimal charge $dq$ on the ring at a distance $z$ from the origin is

$$d\vec E=\frac{dq}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^2}\hat r\tag{B1-1}$$

where $r=(b^2+z^2)^{1/2}$. (B1-2)

($r$ is the distance from a point on the ring to the point $(0,0,z)$.) $\hat r$ is a unit vector at the point $(0,0,z)$ pointing away from the charge $dq$ on the ring.

The $z$-component is then given by:

$$dE_z=dE\cos\theta=\frac{z\,dE}{r}\tag{B1-3}$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between $\hat r$ and the $z$ axis.

Substituting eq. (B1-1) into (B1-2) yields:

$$dE_z=\frac{z\,dq}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^3}.\tag{B1-4}$$

Integrating (B1-4) around the ring and observing that $r$ is the same for all points on the ring yields

$$E_z=\int\frac{z\,dq}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^3}=\frac{zQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^3}.\tag{B1-5}$$

Using the fact that $E_x=E_y=0$ and substituting (B1-2) into (B1-5) gives us the answer.

$$\vec E=E_z\hat k=\frac{zQ\hat k}{4\pi\epsilon_0(b^2+z^2)^{3/2}}.\tag{B1-6}$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
The potential a distance $r$ away from an infinitesimal charge $dq$ is given by

$$dV=\frac{dq}{4\pi\epsilon_0r}.\tag{B1-7}$$

Integrating around the ring, using the fact that $r$ is the same from every point on the ring to the point $(0,0,z)$, and substituting (B1-2) for $r$ yields

$$V=\int\frac{dq}{4\pi\epsilon_0r}=\frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0r}=\frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0(b^2+z^2)^{1/2}}.\tag{B1-8}$$

Note that it is easier to solve part (b) first and then to solve part (a) using

$$E_z=-\frac{dV}{dz}=-\frac d{dz}\left(\frac Q{4\pi\epsilon_0(b^2+z^2)^{1/2}}\right)=-\frac{(-\frac12)(2zQ)}{4\pi\epsilon_0(b^2+z^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{zQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0(b^2+z^2)^{3/2}}.\tag{B1-9}$$

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
The potential energy of the system is given by

$$U=-qV.\tag{B1-10}$$

Using (B1-8),

$$U=\frac{-qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0(b^2+z^2)^{1/2}}.\tag{B1-11}$$

Factoring out $b^2$,

$$U=\frac{-qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0}(b^2+z^2)^{-1/2}=\frac{-qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0b}\left(1+\frac{z^2}{b^2}\right)^{-1/2}.\tag{B1-12}$$

Using the fact that $\lvert z\rvert\ll b$ and using the approximation $(1+x)^n\approx1+nx$ when $x\ll1$, (B1-12) becomes

$$U\approx\frac{-qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0b}\left(1-\frac{z^2}{2b^2}\right).\tag{B1-13}$$

sections.title: d.
sections.statement:
Mechanical energy is conserved, so

$$U(z_0)+K(z_0)=U(0)+K(0).\tag{B1-14}$$

Since the charge is at rest at $z=z_0$ and using (B1-13),

$$\frac{-qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0b}\left(1-\frac{z_0^2}{2b^2}\right)+0=\frac{-qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0b}+\frac12m[v(0)]^2.\tag{B1-15}$$

Solving for $v(0)$,

$$v(0)=\left(\frac{qQz_0^2}{4m\pi\epsilon_0b^3}\right)^{1/2}.\tag{B1-16}$$

sections.title: e.
sections.statement:
We shall use Newton’s Second Law:

$$F_{\rm net}=ma=m\frac{d^2z}{dt^2}.\tag{B1-17}$$

The force on the charge $-q$ is $-qE$ where $E$ is given by (B1-6). Substituting into (B1-17),

$$\frac{-qzQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0(b^2+z^2)^{3/2}}=m\frac{d^2z}{dt^2}.\tag{B1-18}$$

But, $z\ll b$, so $(b^2+z^2)^{3/2}\approx b^3$ and, after dividing both sides by $m$, (B1-18) becomes

$$\frac{d^2z}{dt^2}=\frac{-qQz}{4\pi\epsilon_0mb^3}.\tag{B1-19}$$

We recognize that the differential equation

$$\frac{d^2z}{dt^2}=-\omega^2z\tag{B1-20}$$

is simple harmonic motion. The solution to (B1-20) is

$$z(t)=A\cos\omega t.\tag{B1-21}$$

Since $z(0)=z_0$, we find that $A=z_0$.

By comparison with (B1-19), we find that

$$\omega=\left(\frac{qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0mb^3}\right)^{1/2}.\tag{B1-22}$$

We can derive an expression for the velocity as a function of time by differentiating (B1-21):

$$v(t)=\frac{dz(t)}{dt}=-\omega z_0\sin\omega t\tag{B1-23}$$

(where $\omega$ is given by (B1-22).)

Note that an alternative method of solving part (d) is to note that the speed at the origin will be the maximum value of the magnitude of the velocity

$$v(0)=\omega z_0=\left(\frac{qQz_0^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0mb^3}\right)^{1/2}.$$

Note that an alternative (easier) method of solving part (e) is to note that the potential energy found in (B1-13) is of the form $U(z)=U(0)+kz^2/2$.

Therefore, since it starts from rest, we know that $z(t)=A\cos\omega t$ and that

$$v(t)=\frac{dz(t)}{dt}=-\omega z_0\sin\omega t=-v_{\max}\sin\omega t.$$

Thus, $\omega=v_{\max}/z_0$ and $v_{\max}$ was found in (B1-16).

sections.title: f.
sections.statement:
According to the Biot-Savart law, the magnetic field due to a moving infinitesimal charge $dq$ is given by

$$d\vec B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec s\times\hat r}{r^2}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{dq\,\vec v\times\hat r}{r^2}.\tag{B1-24}$$

Since $d\vec B$ depends on the cross product $\vec v\times\hat r$, $d\vec B$ must be perpendicular to both $\vec v$ and $\hat r$.

By symmetry, when we add the magnetic field vectors due to all points on the rotating ring, the $x$ and $y$ components will cancel. Therefore, we need to find the $z$ components and add them. Let $\phi$ be the angle between $\vec B$ and $\hat z$.

[[figure:p5-fig3]]

$$dB_z=dB\cos\phi=\frac{b\,dB}{r}.\tag{B1-25}$$

Substituting $v=b\omega$ and (B1-24) into (B1-25):

$$dB_z=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{b^2\omega\,dq}{r^3}.\tag{B1-26}$$

Integrating (B1-26) around the ring and observing that $r$ is the same for all points on the ring yields

$$B_z=\int\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{b^2\omega\,dq}{r^3}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{b^2\omega Q}{r^3}.\tag{B1-27}$$

Using the fact that $B_x=B_y=0$ and substituting (B1-2) into (B1-27) gives us the answer.

$$\vec B=B_z\hat k=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{b^2\omega Q\hat k}{(b^2+z^2)^{3/2}}.\tag{B1-28}$$

sections.title: g.
sections.statement:
A point charge $-q$ moving with velocity $\vec v$ in a magnetic field $\vec B$ experiences a magnetic force

$$\vec F_{\rm magn}=-q\vec v\times\vec B.\tag{B1-29}$$

However, since the charge is moving in the $-\hat k$ direction and the magnetic field is in the $\hat k$ direction, $\vec v\times\vec B=0$, so $\vec F_{\rm magn}=0$.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the field at any point on the $z$ axis.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find the potential at any point on the $z$ axis.

sections.title: c.–e.
sections.statement: A point charge with mass $m$ and charge $-q$ is placed at $z=z_0$ where $z_0\ll b$ and released from rest at $t=0$. Ignore any effects due to radiation.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Find the potential energy of the system as a function of $z$, the position of the charge. Expand this potential energy function about the origin for $\lvert z\rvert\le z_0$. Keep only terms to lowest non-zero order in $z$.

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Find the speed of the charge as it passes through the origin.

parts.label: e.
parts.statement: Find the velocity of the charge as a function of time.

sections.title: f.–g.
sections.statement: The point charge is removed and the ring is set into rotation about the $z$-axis with angular velocity $\vec\omega=\omega\hat k$. Ignore any effects due to radiation.

parts.label: f.
parts.statement: Find the magnetic field due to the rotating ring at any point along the $z$-axis.

parts.label: g.
parts.statement: A second point charge with mass $m$ and charge $-q$ is placed at $z=z_0$ where $z_0\ll b$ and released from rest. What is the magnetic force on the charge as it passes through the origin?

problems.statement:
[[figure:p6-fig1]]

A block with uniform density, length $L$, and height $h$, $h\ll L$, starts from rest at the top of a hill of height $H$ as shown in the accompanying diagram. The hill is frictionless and there is a flat frictionless surface at the bottom of the hill that is longer than $L$. Then, there is a flat horizontal surface that has friction. The coefficient of friction between the block and the flat surface with friction is $\mu$. The leading edge of the block comes into contact with the surface with friction when the rest of the block is on a flat frictionless surface.

Express your answers to part (a) in terms of $\mu$, $L$, and $g$.

figures.alt: Block lengthL heighth on frictionless hill of heightH followed by flat frictionless and rough surfaces.

solution.statement: Source note: equations (B2-19), (B2-20), and (B2-25) print time inside square roots; the source’s final stopping-time expression is retained alongside those intermediates. The printed reference to (B2-10) immediately before (B2-23) is also retained.

parts.label: i.
parts.statement:
The frictional force acting on the block depends on the normal force on the portion of the block that is on the rough surface. Therefore,

$$F_{\rm fric}=\frac{\mu xmg}{L}.\tag{B2-1}$$

As the leading edge travels a distance $L$ on the rough surface, friction does work:

$$W_{\rm fric}=\int F_{\rm fric}\,dx=\int_0^L\frac{\mu xmg}{L}\,dx=\frac{\mu Lmg}{2}.\tag{B2-2}$$

Since the block stops after traveling a distance $L$, the work done by friction must equal the initial potential energy of the block.

$$mgH_{\rm crit}=W_{\rm fric}.\tag{B2-3}$$

Using (B2-2), we obtain

$$mgH_{\rm crit}=\frac{\mu Lmg}{2}.\tag{B2-4}$$

Therefore,

$$H_{\rm crit}=\frac{\mu L}{2}.\tag{B2-5}$$

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement:
Substituting (B2-1) into Newton’s Second Law yields:

$$\frac{-\mu xmg}{L}=m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}.\tag{B2-6}$$

Dividing both sides by $m$:

$$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=\frac{-\mu gx}{L}.\tag{B2-7}$$

We recognize that the differential equation

$$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-\omega^2x\tag{B2-8}$$

is simple harmonic motion.

By comparison with (B2-7), we find that

$$\omega=\left(\frac{\mu g}{L}\right)^{1/2}.\tag{B2-9}$$

The period of SHM is $2\pi/\omega$. The motion of the block coming to rest is $\frac14$ of a cycle, so

$$t=\frac T4=\frac\pi2\left(\frac{L}{\mu g}\right)^{1/2}.\tag{B2-10}$$

parts.label: i.
parts.statement:
In this case, the leading edge travels a distance $d$ on the rough surface, so friction does work:

$$W_{\rm fric}=\int F_{\rm fric}\,dx=\int_0^d\frac{\mu xmg}{L}\,dx=\frac{\mu d^2mg}{2L}.\tag{B2-11}$$

Since the block stops after traveling a distance $x$, the work done by friction must equal the initial potential energy of the block.

$$mgH=W_{\rm fric}=\frac{\mu d^2mg}{2L}.\tag{B2-12}$$

Solving for $d$,

$$d=\sqrt{\frac{2HL}{\mu}}.\tag{B2-13}$$

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement: As the block slides on the rough surface, (B2-6) will hold as before. Thus, the motion will be $\frac14$ of a cycle of simple harmonic motion as before. Although the amplitude will be $d$ (given by B2-13) instead of $L$, the period of SHM is independent of the amplitude. Therefore, the time for the block to stop will be the same as (B2-10).

parts.label: i.
parts.statement:
Until the block is entirely on the rough surface, the force of friction acting on the block is given by (B2-1). Once the block is entirely on the surface, the force of friction is constant:

$$F_{\rm fric}=\mu mg.\tag{B2-14}$$

Let $\Delta x=$ the distance that the block travels on the surface with friction after the entire block is on the surface.

We set the initial gravitational potential energy of the block equal to the total work done by friction as the block comes to a stop:

$$mgH=\int_0^L\frac{\mu xmg}{L}\,dx+\mu mg\Delta x.\tag{B2-15}$$

$$mgH=\frac{\mu mgL}{2}+\mu mg\Delta x.\tag{B2-16}$$

Solving for $\Delta x$,

$$\Delta x=\frac H\mu-\frac L2.\tag{B2-17}$$

The total distance traveled by the leading edge across the surface with friction is

$$\Delta x+L=\frac H\mu+\frac L2.\tag{B2-18}$$

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement:
While the block is only partially on the surface with friction, we have SHM as in equation (B2-7). However, since the block does not come to a stop until after the entire block is on the surface, we do not complete one-quarter of the cycle of SHM this time. The solution for SHM is given by

$$x(t)=A\sin\sqrt{\omega t}=A\sin\sqrt{\frac{\mu gt}{L}}\tag{B2-19}$$

where we have used (B2-9).

Take the derivative of (B2-19) to find velocity:

$$v(t)=A\sqrt{\frac{\mu g}{L}}\cos\sqrt{\frac{\mu gt}{L}}.\tag{B2-20}$$

We can find the velocity of the block just before the leading edge hits the surface with friction using conservation of mechanical energy:

$$mgH=\frac{mv^2}{2}.\tag{B2-21}$$

$$v=\sqrt{2gH}.\tag{B2-22}$$

We can evaluate the amplitude $A$ by substituting (B2-22) for $v$ when $t=0$ into (B2-10):

$$\sqrt{2gH}=A\sqrt{\frac{\mu g}{L}}.\tag{B2-23}$$

$$A=\sqrt{\frac{2HL}{\mu}}.\tag{B2-24}$$

Let $t_1$ be the time that it takes the leading edge of the block to travel a distance $L$ across the surface with friction. To find $t_1$, we substitute (B2-24) into (B2-19) and solve for $t$.

$$L=\sqrt{\frac{2HL}{\mu}}\sin\sqrt{\frac{\mu gt}{L}}.\tag{B2-25}$$

$$t_1=\sqrt{\frac L{\mu g}}\sin^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{\mu L}{2H}}.\tag{B2-26}$$

Now, that the entire block is on the surface with friction, we need to find the additional time that it will take to stop it. Now that the entire block is on the surface, the force, and therefore the acceleration, are constant. We need to find out how fast the block is going at the instant that the leading edge has traveled a distance $L$. We shall use the generalized work-energy theorem where the work done by friction is given by (B2-2).

$$mgH=\frac{\mu mgL}{2}+\frac{mv^2}{2}.\tag{B2-27}$$

Solving for $v$,

$$v=\sqrt{2gH-\mu gL}.\tag{B2-28}$$

From (B2-14), we see that the acceleration of the block is given by

$$a=-\mu g.\tag{B2-29}$$

Let $t_2=$ the time that it takes the block to come to rest after the entire block is on the surface with friction. Using the definition of acceleration and (B2-29) and (B2-28) we have

$$t_2=\frac{0-v}{a}=\frac{-\sqrt{2gH-\mu gL}}{-\mu g}=\sqrt{\frac{2H}{g\mu^2}-\frac L{\mu g}}.\tag{B2-30}$$

The total time that it takes to stop is then given by adding (B2-26) and (B2-30).

$$t=t_1+t_2=\sqrt{\frac L{\mu g}}\sin^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{\mu L}{2H}}+\sqrt{\frac{2H}{g\mu^2}-\frac L{\mu g}}.\tag{B2-31}$$

sections.title: a.
sections.statement: If the hill has a certain critical height, $H_{\rm crit}$, the block comes to a stop at the instant that the entire block is on the surface with friction. (This is the instant at which the leading edge has traveled a distance $L$ across the surface with friction).

parts.label: i.
parts.statement: Find the critical height $H_{\rm crit}$.

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement: If the hill has the critical height found in part (i), what is the time from the instant that the leading edge of the block encounters friction until the block comes to a stop?

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
Express your answers to parts (b) and (c) in terms of $H$, $\mu$, $L$, and $g$.

If the hill has a height $H<H_{\rm crit}$:

parts.label: i.
parts.statement: Find the distance that the leading edge of the block travels across the surface with friction before it comes to a stop.

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement: Find the time from the instant that the leading edge of the block encounters friction until the block comes to a stop.

sections.title: c.
sections.statement: If the hill has a height $H>H_{\rm crit}$:

parts.label: i.
parts.statement: Find the distance that the leading edge of the block travels across the surface with friction before it comes to a stop.

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement: Find the time from the instant that the leading edge of the block encounters friction until the block comes to a stop.
